conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m Dr. Martinez, one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. I’ll be spending a few minutes with you today to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived.

We routinely use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short**. It’s simply a way to hear, in your own words, how things have been going emotionally over the past week. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about safety. Our goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported.

I’ll ask you 10 questions, one at a time, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to start?

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Oh, yeah, I can still laugh—maybe not as easily as before the baby came, but when my husband makes a goofy face or when the dog does something silly, I’ll still crack up. It’s not every single day, but it happens.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I still find something to giggle at—like yesterday when my little guy shot a fountain of spit-up straight onto Dad’s clean shirt. I chuckled, even if it was followed by a tired sigh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Yeah, I still get excited about little stuff—like the afternoon walk we take most days or my favorite show once the baby’s finally down. I might be tired, but I do look forward to those moments.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if I’m late getting a bottle ready and he starts wailing, I might think, “Ugh, I could’ve planned better,” but it’s just a passing thought. I don’t sit around beating myself up about it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit, yeah. Mostly it’s just tiny flashes—like I’ll suddenly worry if he’s breathing when he’s napping, or I’ll replay in my head whether I buckled the car seat right. It’s not all the time and it’s not overwhelming, just quick “what-if” moments that pass once I check on him.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt that kind of sudden panic. Sometimes a little anxious flicker about the baby, but it’s not that scared, heart-racing feeling for no reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

Now and then, sure—like when the laundry pile looks like a mountain and he decides to have a blow-out right as I’m walking out the door. For a minute it feels like “ugh, everything’s happening at once,” but once I tackle one thing it calms back down. Overall I’m keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, nothing like that. I’m tired at the end of the day, but once I crawl into bed I fall asleep pretty easily. I haven’t felt so upset that it kept me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable
I’ve had a couple of teary moments—mostly when I’m really tired and he won’t settle—but they pass quickly. I wouldn’t say I feel generally sad or miserable; it’s more like fleeting frustration.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I’ve teared up once or twice when the baby was fussy and I was running on fumes, but it was just for a minute and then I moved on. I haven’t had any big crying spells.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never—nothing like that has crossed my mind.

You shared that, overall, you're still finding moments to laugh and look forward to your daily walk or favorite show, even though life with a newborn can feel hectic. Occasional <sym>worry flashes</sym> about the baby's safety pop up, and every so often the laundry pile or a diaper blow-out leaves you briefly overwhelmed or teary, but these feelings pass quickly and have not affected your sleep or general mood. You clearly love your little one and are coping well, asking only for reassurance that what you're experiencing is normal.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 7, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient describes specific recurrent worries without clear trigger, occurring "sometimes" in quick flashes, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> criteria: low scores on anhedonia, low mood, guilt, sleep disturbance, self-harm ideation; only Q4 (anxiety) and Q6 (coping) show mild elevation. Total 7 falls well below the 9-point threshold for possible depression. Symptoms are context-specific, brief, and without functional impairment, more consistent with normative <med>postpartum adjustment</med> than a depressive or anxiety disorder. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine pediatric and postpartum check-ups; mention any mood changes at visits
2. Practice brief self-care: accept help with chores, schedule the daily walk, use 5-minute breathing when <sym>worry flashes</sym> arise
3. Keep a simple log of tearful or anxious moments; if frequency or duration increases, re-screen in 2-4 weeks
4. Maintain open dialogue-call the office anytime you feel persistently down, panicky, or have thoughts of self-harm
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 7: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item self-report (EPDS-style) + brief clarifications

Symptoms endorsed  
- Mild, situational anxious “what-if” flashes about infant safety (Q4)  
- Transient feeling of being overwhelmed when multiple tasks collide (Q6)  
- Occasional tired-related tearfulness, quickly resolving (Q8–Q9)

Symptoms denied  
- Persistent low mood, loss of pleasure, excessive guilt, sleep-mood linkage, panic, self-harm ideation (Q1–3, 5, 7, 10)

Pattern  
Generally positive affect preserved; stress reactions context-specific, short-lived, without functional impairment or safety concern.

Screening significance  
Current responses do not indicate clinically significant depression or anxiety. Continue routine postpartum monitoring; educate on normative emotional changes and when to re-contact services.
